column2: Has your daily routine been regular lately?
Regular — I sleep and wake at about the same time every day
Mostly regular; later nights and mornings on weekends
Very irregular (shift work, frequent late nights, jet lag)
On normal days (work or class days), do you need an alarm to wake up?
Hardly ever — I wake up naturally on time
I need an alarm, but I get up
I need an alarm and often hit snooze
After waking up, how long until your mind is fully clear?
Within 15 minutes
About half an hour
About an hour
More than an hour
From after lunch until 3 pm, how are you usually?
Sleepy or distracted almost every day
Sometimes
Rarely affected
Without phone distractions, how long can you focus on one thing at a time?
15–25 minutes
25–45 minutes
45+ minutes
During breaks, what restores you best?
Choose any
Getting up to walk or stretch
A 10–20 minute nap
A snack or some water
Chatting with someone
Music or zoning out
Scenario 1: You have a very important exam tomorrow and can choose the time. Which time slot would you pick?
Choose 1–2
Scenario 2: You need to write a report or paper that requires deep thinking, with no rush and full freedom to schedule. When does your writing usually flow best?
Scenario 3: Think of the last time you were completely absorbed and lost track of time (studying, writing, problem-solving all count). Roughly what time was it?
Choose 1–2; if you can't remember, pick the closest
When do ideas most often pop up? (e.g. in the shower, on a walk, right before sleep)
When are you most likely to get distracted, make mistakes, or be unable to get anything done?
Self-direction
Choosing and cultivating your own ideas, views and actions
I like to think and do things my own way, choosing my own goals and methods.
I need freedom; I don't like others planning every step for me.
You need to feel “I chose this.” With clear goals and your own methods, you're at your strongest; when rules are too rigid, you push back.
Agree on the expected outcome with your teacher or manager, but decide the method yourself
Each week, choose next week's materials and practice methods yourself
Protect uninterrupted time blocks on your calendar
Batch admin and chores into fixed time slots
Too many options means time lost to planning. Plan for 10 minutes max, then start.
Is someone dictating the method too rigidly?
Negotiate to do at least part of it your own way
Stimulation
Novelty, excitement and challenge in life
I like a fresh, exciting, challenging life and often want to try new things.
Unchanging days feel dull to me; I like surprises and variety.
Novelty is your fuel. Too much repetition drains your motivation; some variety pulls you back in.
Prepare two or three ways to practice for the same goal and rotate them
Change location, change the order, or challenge yourself against the clock
Keep the big framework fixed, with variety inside it
Schedule a small exploration in each block as a reward
New things can pull you away before you finish. Write new ideas down first; start them after finishing what's in hand.
Is this task too monotonous or repetitive?
Change location or method, or give yourself a timed challenge
Hedonism
Enjoying life's pleasures, especially sensory ones
I care a lot about enjoying life — good food, music and comfortable surroundings.
Being able to relax properly and treat myself matters to me.
Enjoyment is how you recharge. Schedule pleasure into your plan instead of waiting until you can't hold on and then overindulging.
Make your study space comfortable: a nice drink, music you like
Give yourself a concrete small treat after each block
Schedule some “intentional indulgence” each week and treat it as a fixed appointment
Start the workday with a pleasant ritual
Relaxing without limits easily turns into procrastination. Set a time first, and stop when it's up.
Have I gone too long without a break?
Schedule a deliberate break first, then come back
Achievement
Succeeding, by your own standards or others'
I really want to succeed and to have my abilities proven.
Seeing myself achieve results and become more capable energizes me most.
Progress and results are your most direct motivation. Goals just above your current ability excite you.
Set a specific numeric goal before each practice
Make progress visible with stats and trend charts
Write each goal in two versions: a stretch version and a minimum version
Break big goals into weekly milestones you can check off
When results disappoint, you may be hard on yourself. Track effort too, not just outcomes.
Can't see progress or results on this?
Break it into small goals you can check off
Power
Control over material and social resources, or influence over others
I want to control resources, make decisions, or have influence over others.
In a group, I want my opinion to carry weight and to steer the direction.
You're most engaged when you're in charge. Being able to decide and affect outcomes makes you more willing to take responsibility.
Take the lead in a study group or practice group
Be the “owner” of your study plan and review it regularly
Ask for a part you're responsible for and can make decisions on
Use your influence to bring resources together, not to control people
Wanting too much control can lead to conflict. First check which things really need your decision.
Do I have no say at all in this?
Find a part you can own and decide on
Face
Maintaining your image and avoiding embarrassment
I care about my image and don't want to lose face in front of others.
Failing in public or being criticized is especially hard for me.
You care how you're seen. That makes you value quality, but fear of being seen doing badly can also make you procrastinate.
Practice somewhere private first; bring it out once you're comfortable
Treat mistakes as private practice material, not as scores
Write a private draft first and show only one or two trusted people
Schedule an early “small-audience run-through” to lower the pressure of the real thing
Striving to never make mistakes delays getting started. Finish a rough version first, then refine.
Am I afraid of being seen doing badly?
Make a private draft first and show only one or two trusted people
Security
Safety and stability in your environment and society
I value safety and stability; I like life to be predictable and secure.
Before deciding, I first make sure I have a fallback and safeguards.
Stability and security let you move forward with peace of mind. With enough security you dare to go for it; without it, you hold back.
Start early and leave yourself a buffer
Learn the rules of the exam or task first to reduce uncertainty
Prepare a fallback plan for every challenge
List the worst case and the backup plan — once written down, it stops nagging you
Only seeking safety can mean missing worthwhile challenges. Add a safety net rather than giving up.
Is this too unfamiliar or uncertain?
Design a minimum version first, or ask someone experienced
Tradition
Appreciating, preserving and continuing cultural, family and religious customs and rituals
I value and want to keep family, cultural or religious customs and rituals.
Holidays, family gatherings and regular rituals have special meaning for me.
Heritage and belonging give you strength. You're especially willing to invest in things connected to your traditions, beliefs or mentors.
Build a fixed study ritual, e.g. starting at the same time and place every day
Ask seniors or mentors how they do it
Write down how this task connects to the heritage you value
Turn key milestones into moments with a sense of ritual
Relying too much on old methods can leave you stuck in new situations. Keep the core, adapt the method.
Has this become disconnected from the heritage or beliefs I value?
Find its connection to your traditions, mentors or beliefs
Conformity
Following rules, obligations and expectations; avoiding harming or offending others
I keep rules and promises even when no one is watching.
I try not to do things that make others uncomfortable or disappointed.
Clear rules and commitments help you move forward steadily. You also care about not being a burden to others.
Practice from a clear schedule or spec
Make commitments to others, e.g. agree on progress with a study buddy
Confirm standards, format and deadlines before you start
Tell the people involved about your deadline and let the commitment push you
Caring too much about others' expectations can make you forget what you want. Ask yourself now and then: is this what I want?
Am I unsure what others expect of me?
Confirm the standards and deadline first, then follow a clear spec
Humility
Recognizing your smallness in the wider world and feeling part of a larger whole
I know I'm small in the wider world, and I feel part of a larger whole.
When things don't go as planned, I can accept it without insisting on my own way.
You can accept things as they are and take gains and losses lightly, which keeps you steadier through setbacks.
Treat each practice as part of a process, without rushing to prove yourself
Ask people better than you for advice, without fear of looking ignorant
Remind yourself: one failure is a small step in a long process
Put your results in a bigger context and consider their place in the whole
Accepting things too easily may mean missing chances worth fighting for. Speak up about what matters.
Am I taking this too seriously, caring too much about winning or losing?
Remind yourself it's a small step in the process — finish it first
Universalism
Understanding, appreciating and protecting the welfare of all people and nature
I care about the welfare of all people and nature, and value fairness and inclusion.
Injustice or environmental damage really bothers me.
Meaning and fairness drive you. When you know the value of something for the world and for more people, you find the energy.
Choose materials related to issues you care about
Imagine who you could help once you've learned this
Write down which people or causes this work will ultimately help
Act within your means; you don't have to do it perfectly all at once
Chores that feel meaningless keep getting postponed. Batch them into low-energy times and clear them.
Can't see what this means for the world?
Write down which people or cause it will ultimately help
Benevolence
Being a reliable, loyal member and caring for those around you
I want to be reliable and trustworthy and to take care of the people who matter to me.
When friends or family need me, helping them comes first.
Deep relationships are a source of strength. When you do it for people you care about, you're less likely to give up.
Find one or two study buddies to cheer each other on
Teach what you've learned to people you care about
Think about who it will help once it's done, and write it next to the goal
Share progress with people close to you — no need to go public
You tend to look after others first and neglect your own progress. Treat your own time blocks as commitments too.
Does this have nothing to do with the people I care about?
Think about who it will help, or ask a friend to do it with you

Dig into something I've always wanted to explore
Go somewhere I've never been
Sleep well, eat good food, binge a show

Keeping an important family or group tradition alive

Always go home — it matters to me
Take the chance to relax and enjoy

How embarrassing — I hope no one noticed
I'll definitely do better next time
Everyone makes mistakes; just improve

There's a risky but promising opportunity:
Go for it! New challenges are exciting
First check the worst case and a way out
Take it if it moves me up a level
Ask family or mentors for their opinion first

I want to understand and do something
I see it through my faith or culture
I feel one person can only do so much, but I do my best

What kind of day feels most “worth it”:
A comfortable, pleasant one
One where I completed something I led
One where I handled myself well and earned recognition
One where I helped someone
When joining a new group, what do you care about most:
The group's traditions and rules
Making a good impression
Observing quietly first, not rushing to stand out
Whether everyone is treated fairly and included
What's a goal you recently completed? Why do you think you managed it?
What kind of task do you procrastinate on most? Which part of it makes you resist?
After completing your most important current goal, what are you most looking forward to?
When you're in a bad state, what helps you recover most?
